articles.title: Apple Trained Own AI Model for China Market With Help From Alibaba
articles.subtitle: Reuters reports that Apple has trained its own large language model for the China market, rather than relying on a third-party model to power its Apple Intelligence features in the country.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Reuters reports that Apple has trained its own large language model for the China market, rather than relying on a third-party model to power its Apple Intelligence features in the country.

The LLM has been developed with the help of Alibaba, according to the report's sources. The development marks a break from Apple's previous strategy of relying on domestic models to bring generative AI to its devices sold in China.

Rollout of its AI features in China is expected in the coming months. The rollout is described by the report as a "dual-track strategy" for AI deployment in China, allowing Apple to navigate regulatory hurdles that have limited access for other U.S. tech companies.

The move makes Apple the first foreign company approved by the Chinese government to offer a proprietary AI model in the country.

Apple previously agreed with Chinese regulators to incorporate Alibaba's Qwen model into Apple Intelligence features, similar to Apple's existing ChatGPT extension available elsewhere. Apple briefly published a support guide in China explaining how Mac users can connect Alibaba's Qwen AI to Siri and Writing Tools, before pulling it entirely less than a day later.

articles.title: Review: SuperDuper! 4 gets a stem-to-stern revamp, but is just as seaworthy as ever
articles.subtitle: Backups, as any computer user knows, are worth their weight in gold. If it isn’t backed up, it might as well might not exist. That’s why I have for years trusted ShirtPocket’s SuperDuper!…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Backups, as any computer user knows, are worth their weight in gold. If it isn’t backed up, it might as well might not exist. That’s why I have for years trusted ShirtPocket’s SuperDuper! to ensure that all my data is safe and sound. And now, for the first time in a very long time, the venerable backup utility has gotten a top-to-bottom update that brings it into the modern era without sacrificing any of the features—and, most importantly, the reliability—that its users have come to depend on.

While SuperDuper! 4 may look like an entirely new beast, its history has stuck around. It still explains what it’s doing in plain English. It still allows you to make complete, bootable backups. It still has its excellent Smart Update option to optimize the copying process.

But it’s gotten some significant updates too. There’s a new interface, for starters, which conforms to Apple’s current Liquid Glass aesthetic, love it or hate it. It’s a bit of a shock to the system after so long without a change, but it’s hard to deny that the old look had grown somewhat antiquated. The result is an app that makes backups as simple and straightforward as they should be, so that anyone can figure it out: click here to set your destination, choose what method, and click Go.

The changes to SuperDuper! 4 also run more than just skin deep. For example, it’s considerably faster than the previous version—up to an order magnitude faster using the new Turbo implementation of Smart Update, according to Shirt Pocket. That’s borne out in my real-world usage. For example, my last nightly backup of 20.55GB took less than 4 minutes.

There are new capabilities here, too. A new Preview feature lets you perform a dry run of your copy job, letting you see every file that will be changed without actually doing any of it. With a new background helper app, copies won’t interrupt whatever you’re doing. And there’s Shortcuts support, so you can run a workflow when your copy job is completed—or even have one of your shortcuts kick off a copy job.

I’ve been using betas of SuperDuper! 4 for a month or so now, and what’s impressed me most is how much it maintains that set-it-and-forget-it strength of the previous versions. The most important thing for a backup is that element of reliability, so when I open up the app and see “31 successful in a row” note, I know that my data is right where it should be.

And if something goes wrong, it’s easier than ever to see what happened: click on a failed job and you’ll get the details, including an Apple Intelligence-powered summary of the job. (You can get that for completed jobs too. )

There are way more features here too, ones that I just don’t have much reason to use for my purposes, but might just well be what you’re looking for. For example, copy rules that let you handle certain files and folders in granular ways, such as excluding certain ones from backups; support for any file system that macOS understands; and there’s support for multiple copy jobs at the same time, even for those that are scheduled.

Backup apps may not be the most exciting software category, but I dare you to find one that’s more crucial. For me, SuperDuper! has done the job for years and I’ve never had any reason to complain about it. Nothing about that seems poised to change with version 4.

SuperDuper! 4 requires macOS 14 (Sonoma) or later. A free trial version lets you make unlimited full erase backups, but to unlock the rest of the features requires a one-time payment of $43.95. There’s also an upgrade discount for owners of SuperDuper 3 of up to 30 percent. (And, if you bought version 3 very recently, you may be able to get version 4 for free.) And good news: if you need to run backups on older systems, SuperDuper 3 is sticking around.

For everybody who’s already backing up their Macs, SuperDuper! 4 may offer some new features and speed increases that will make the process even smoother. For those of you who aren’t yet…what are you waiting for?

articles.title: ChatGPT for Mac adds opt-in Computer History feature, replacing Chronicle
articles.subtitle: OpenAI is giving ChatGPT and Codex a new way to learn from and remember how you use your Mac, even when that work happens outside the app.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
OpenAI is giving ChatGPT and Codex a new way to learn from and remember how you use your Mac, even when that work happens outside the app.

ChatGPT Computer History is an upgraded replacement for Codex’s Chronicle research preview

The new Computer History feature builds a searchable timeline from activity across selected apps and websites.

OpenAI announced Computer History in Thursday’s desktop app changelog. The feature is off by default and must be enabled by each user, giving people control over which sources contribute to their history.

The release comes a month after Codex joined ChatGPT on the desktop. It also follows OpenAI’s experimental Chronicle feature from earlier this year.

OpenAI says Computer History actually replaces the Chronicle research preview, but calls it a rebuilt system rather than a simple rename.

Chronicle relied on screenshots. Computer History instead records interaction events exposed through macOS accessibility features, including clicks, typing, keyboard shortcuts, and switching between apps.

Today we're releasing Computer History in ChatGPT. It lets ChatGPT learn from everything you do on your computer, so it can better understand how you work, finish tasks that you're in the middle of, and suggest skills and automations based on how you use your computer. pic.twitter.com/xnTq7hWH8O — Ari Weinstein (@AriX) August 13, 2026

Here’s how OpenAI describes the new feature:

Computer History is an opt-in feature in the ChatGPT desktop app on macOS that turns activity across apps and websites into memories and a timeline that ChatGPT and Codex can use. Choose which apps and websites contribute, pause collection, and review or delete your history at any time. Computer History is available to ChatGPT Pro, Business, and Enterprise users.

Business and Enterprise administrators must enable access before workspace members can turn it on. Initial availability excludes the European Economic Area (EEA), Switzerland, and the United Kingdom.

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

Another endorsement of Apple’s approach

articles.title: Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls review
articles.subtitle: Performance anxiety.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
Arc System Works can do just about anything, including convincing me to pick up a Marvel-themed 2D anime fighter. Not that I've got anything particularly against either of those things. But as someone who grew up firmly in the 3D fighting game scene (and continues to dwell there) and traditionally doesn't care much for superheroes beyond Spider-Man, Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls should be a hard sell for someone like me.

What is it? A 4v4 tag fighter chock-full of super-jacked heroes

Release date August 6, 2026

Expect to pay $60 / £60

Developer Arc System Works

Publisher PlayStation Publishing LLC

Reviewed on Nvidia GeForce RTX3070, AMD Ryzen 9 3900XT, 32GB RAM

Steam Deck Unsupported

Multiplayer? Yes

Link: Official site

And yet Arc System Works has utterly enamoured me to its riff on both the Marvel universe and tag fighters, having me grumble significantly less about anti-airs and jump cancels than I traditionally would. Its low skill floor and high skill ceiling leaves tons of room for expression, from casual autocombo mashers to professionals who can hit you with a two-touch death combo if you're not careful.

Avengers Assemble

Whereas most tag fighters are a conservative 2v2 or 3v3 battle, Marvel Tōkon pits a whopping four characters against each other. That would be downright terrifying by usual tag fighter rules—learning two characters has put more than enough folks off the likes of Tekken Tag Tournament and 2XKO—but Tōkon grounds its larger teams by giving all characters a shared health bar.

It means you can essentially play Tōkon as a 1v1 with the odd assist here and there, while letting you go ham with a full team if you want to. But the game doesn't give you access to all four outright. Instead, you'll start with two characters, continuing to build out your team throughout the match through things like stage breaks, wall splats, and… well, losing the round. It folds in an element of strategy that I really like and stops Tōkon from feeling like a total snowball fest.

Its roster of characters is genuinely stellar, too. Each fighter is already loosely grouped up into a team—you've got the classic Avengers with Captain America, Iron Man, Black Panther, and Hulk. My personal favourite is the Samurai Outlaws comp made up of Ghost Rider (I am now a little obsessed with Robbie Reyes), Blade, Deadpool, and Loki.

Arc System Works has done such a fantastic job of making each character's moveset fit with their personality. Spider-Man thwips around the stage with his webs, Magik can go for an all-out assault from her portals, and Deadpool's penchant for being all meta absolutely shines through his moveset—essentially chock-full of easter eggs like Kauzya's Electric Wind God Fist, the Jack-O crouching pose, and Scorpion's signature "Get over here!"

I'm grateful to see Arc System Works incorporating both its regular motion inputs and a more simplified control scheme similar to Granblue Fantasy Versus: Rising here as well—allowing newer players to forgo quarter-circles in favour of basic directional inputs and a special button. The trade-off is a little less damage than going for the classic method, but it's one that makes Tōkon far more approachable from the get-go, a problem that fighting games often struggle with.

articles.title: What to do when a macOS update goes wrong
articles.subtitle: Anything can happen, but so long as you have a recent backup you should be able fix the problems and get back up and running again. Here's how.
articles.author: The Eclectic Light Company
articles.content:
While macOS updates have become increasingly reliable, the more updates you install, the greater the chances of one of them going wrong. Because they can change components from the firmware to bundled apps and Safari, those post-update problems can include anything from kernel panics to Finder glitches.

The single most important action you should take before starting any macOS update, no matter how small, is to check that you have a current backup. If you have Time Machine or a third-party equivalent set to make hourly backups, this should be no more than a quick check to ensure there’s a backup in storage that was made in the last hour. If full backups are less frequent then you may need to make a fresh one before going any further.

Another good habit of the past, running First Aid on your startup disk, should no longer be necessary, though. To do that properly you’d need to start up in Recovery and run it from there. This was almost essential in the years before journalling was added to HFS+, to ensure there were no minor errors that could escalate to a disaster in the update. With APFS First Aid is only indicated when you suspect there may be a problem with the file system of the boot volume group to be updated.

There’s one emergency situation that can happen on rare occasions if there has been a problem updating firmware: a boot loop, in which the Mac tries to start up, hits an early kernel panic, so tries to restart again, and continues in that loop. If that happens, press and hold the Power button until the Mac shuts down, and refer to this article.

macOS Tahoe introduced a new Recovery mode, Device Recovery Assistant. When your Mac has problems starting up correctly, it may start up in this new mode to perform repairs, and should also capture a sysdiagnose in the process. This is described here.

Otherwise the first thing to try is simply restarting your Mac normally. If that proves a problem, or things are still awry, try Safe mode. On an Apple silicon Mac, shut it down, wait ten seconds or so, then start it up in Recovery, select the disk to use for Safe mode, hold the Shift key, and click Continue in Safe Mode.

On an Intel Mac, hold the Shift key during startup.

Once running, leave your Mac for a couple of minutes, then restart in normal mode, with your fingers tightly crossed.

Sometimes Safe mode works fine, but as soon as you return to normal mode everything goes wrong again. That’s a good indicator that something you have installed is at fault, rather than the macOS update, although it’s often a combination of both working against one another. You now need to hunt down the third-party software that has become upset by the update, and either update or remove it.

If Safe mode either doesn’t help, or you can’t even enter it, then your Mac’s problems could be from the macOS update itself or something third-party, and teasing them apart isn’t going to be easy. This is when you should, for the first time, ask yourself whether you want to return to your previous version of macOS without the update, or try to fix what you’ve got. You can change your mind later, but this is a key question determining what you do next.

In all more serious problems following a macOS update, now’s the time to gather evidence that could be useful later, particularly if you need to call on Apple Support. The best way to do this is to run a sysdiagnose, which captures the contents of your Mac’s log before relevant entries are removed, and adds to that detailed information about everything else that could be relevant to engineers investigating the problem.

There are three ways to create a sysdiagnose for a Mac:

Using both hands, press Command-Option-Control-Shift-. [period or stop] at the same time.

In Activity Monitor’s toolbar, open the … [ellipsis] menu and select the System Diagnostics command.

In Terminal, type the command sudo sysdiagnose, although I prefer using sudo sysdiagnose -f ~/Documents to save the archive in my Documents folder. You will be shown a stern warning and have to press Enter to confirm you really do want to create the archive.

Several minutes later, you should be shown where the sysdiagnose archive has been saved, normally in /var/tmp/ unless you use the -f option at the command line. Copy that to external storage if possible, so you’ll retain access even if the boot disk is completely erased when trying to fix the problem.

Rarely, you may discover that some files or even whole apps appear to have vanished from your Mac when it logs you back in after an update. In most cases, these have been moved to the Trash, and should still be there as long as you haven’t emptied it. It’s most unusual, though, for anything to simply disappear.

Before macOS Catalina, you’d be right to suspect this might have occurred as a result of the macOS update. Since Big Sur, it has become more likely to be an unfortunate side-effect. In those more recent versions, for almost the whole duration of the update, the Data volume containing your files and apps is unmounted, as all the action takes place on the System volume and those in hidden containers.

articles.title: Big Walk: A Good Hang with Friends
articles.subtitle: I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it. And because most of my gaming is done solo, I initially tuned out most of the game’s post-launch headlines. Still, Big Walk is published by Panic, which has a great track record for finding and publishing great indie games, so I decided to give it a try earlier this week. And you know what? I love it.

Big Walk is about as low-key as a puzzle game gets in the best possible way. Co-op is the only mode, so you’ll need to coordinate a time to play it with a friend or group. One person takes the lead, setting up the session and inviting the others. The process is far simpler than trying to find a time that works for everyone in your group.

As players join, you’re dropped into a space to wait for the others and explore a little. This lobby space is where you’ll learn the game’s controls, too. Big Walk supports keyboard and mouse input as well as a controller, which is what I used, playing on an M4 Max MacBook Pro.

Once you get your bearings, it’s time to exit the lobby and start exploring. That exploration is core to what Big Walk is all about. You aren’t told what to do, but there are just enough clues to push you forward, figuring out the goals on your own without too much trouble.

I played using AirPods Pro 3, and the game made great use of their mics and speakers, simulating the environments we were in. Closed spaces were echoey, and speech was distant and faint when we were separated. Sound even becomes part of the mechanic in some puzzles, such as an early one where you have to look through an open window to hear each other properly and help guide the other player’s actions.

That cooperation is the key part of the game’s loop. You may see how to solve Big Walk’s puzzles on your own, but implementing the solution will require you and a companion to work together.

The togetherness of it all extends beyond the puzzles, too. Big Walk’s environment (at least in the early stages) is mountainous with large rocks and trees that make it possible to get separated from others. Add to that day and night cycles where it’s almost impossible to see where you’re going at night without a light, and you have every incentive not to wander off on your own without a plan for how to reconnect.

I’ve played through Big Walk’s first couple of sections, and it was a blast. The puzzles were clever and challenging without being frustrating, but most of all, I enjoyed working through them with someone else. There’s no time pressure or monsters lurking around corners – just puzzles and a chance to chat.

Ultimately, that’s what makes Big Walk work. It’s a good hang built against the backdrop of a beautiful landscape and low-key, fun challenges. I highly recommend giving it a try.

Big Walk, which supports crossplay and 2–12 players, is available on the Mac App Store for $14.99. The game is also on Steam, the Switch 2, and PS5.

articles.title: AAPL stock rallies 15% as investors favor AI caution and welcome price increases
articles.subtitle: Apple stock slid significantly downwards in the wake of the WWDC keynote, with some attributing that to disappointment in the company’s AI announcements.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Apple stock slid significantly downwards in the wake of the WWDC keynote, with some attributing that to disappointment in the company’s AI announcements.

While we disagreed with that analysis, investors do now seem to be welcoming the company’s caution when it comes to AI spending, with the stock rallying 15% since that June low …

The company’s shares slid 4% the day after the keynote, but there were a number of macroeconomic factors affecting a wide range of stocks at the same time, including US strikes against Iran after the downing of an American helicopter.

The stock has rallied even more substantially since then, pushing it back into record territory. Bloomberg believes that AI is a factor in this, albeit somewhat indirectly. It suggests that investors are growing increasingly skeptical about AI spending by other companies and says that Apple’s more cautious approach is now seen as a positive.

The stock’s reversal reflects rising unease about the prospects for heavy spending on AI paying off, with Apple’s decision not to participate in the data center arms race increasingly being viewed as an asset, rather than a liability, even though its AI offerings have repeatedly frustrated investors.

“There’s a battle in the market, and right now Apple is benefiting because it isn’t in the storm that the rest of the AI trade is in,” said Mark Bronzo, chief investment strategist at Rye Strategic Partners. “People are concerned about what kind of return hyperscalers could get from their AI spending [and] as a result, investors have gravitated back to Apple as a steady-eddy name without those risks. ”

articles.title: GameSir T7 Pro Sugar Whirl review
articles.subtitle: Not quite the sweetest of treats.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
First, let me admit my biases: Yes, this controller's raspberry ripple blend of pink, blue, and purple really does work for me. That said, the GameSir T7 Pro Sugar Whirl has more going for it than just pretty face buttons, featuring TMR sticks alongside Hall effect triggers. Gorgeous and precise, this is also a wireless controller that's actually compatible with the notoriously picky Xbox consoles.

Speaking of an untethered experience, this gamepad's charging situation annoys me significantly less than other wireless options. Basically, as someone with a perennially cluttered desk, I didn't think I'd ever be pro charging docks. However, this GameSir gamepad has finally shown me the light.

Thanks to the charging dock, the T7 Pro offers a pretty seamless wireless experience. That ease of use extends to the refreshingly straightforward software package, which offers a wealth of options to make this Pro pad feel your own. Beyond deadzone tweaking and even motion control fiddling, I personally could have done with just a few more RGB lighting customisation options.

Unfortunately, the ergonomic design of the T7 Pro may not play well with tiny hand bandits such as myself. Make no mistake, this is far from the heftiest or chunkiest wireless controller. As such, I was surprised to find that certain button placements strained my small palms.

Furthermore, with a $90/£100, I have the nagging feeling I'm simply paying more for the cute colourway and a bit of extra connectivity I probably won't even use. The simple fact is that if you're not fussed about either RGB lighting or wireless Xbox connectivity, you can get a great Pro pad for less than this asking price.

articles.title: Apple’s revolving door continues to spin, with more big-name exec changes
articles.subtitle: Macworld Apple is a large and wealthy company which employs roughly 166,000 people, so a fair amount of staff turnover is to be expected.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Apple is a large and wealthy company which employs roughly 166,000 people, so a fair amount of staff turnover is to be expected. What’s striking about the past couple of years, however, has been the number of employees leaving high-profile roles at Apple Park.

Last December, Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman discussed what he called Apple’s “biggest personnel shake-up in decades,” listing 18 big-name departures that had either happened that year or were expected to happen soon. By February, the situation had become so noticeable that CEO Tim Cook was moved to comment, sagely observing that “when people get to a certain age, some are going to retire. This is kind of a natural thing,” and insisting that the departures had been carefully orchestrated.

Whether planned or not, the high-profile personnel changes keep coming, with two more emerging this week.

First, Apple internally announced the retirement of Jennifer Bailey, who has been at the company for more than two decades, most recently as head of Pay and Wallet services. In an article revealing the move, Gurman claimed Bailey’s exit “is seen as a major loss within Apple, according to people with knowledge of the move” and that staff fears it will “presage a broader exodus of senior leaders in their 60s.

” Bailey will retire in October, although services boss Eddy Cue (current age: 61) insists she will continue in an advisory role and that a succession plan will be announced nearer the time. The current lack of a succession plan (or disinclination to reveal one) hints that this departure was less orchestrated, but there may be other factors we don’t know about.

Second, and more positively, it was announced (again by Mark Gurman at Bloomberg ) that Apple is hiring a new head of government affairs. Nate Gatten, formerly an exec at American Airlines, will take on this “delicate role,” for which his Republican ties are likely to be seen as an advantage.

A big-name signing is a win, of course, but there are complications. For one thing, this is connected to another retirement: legal chief Katherine Adams is leaving at the same time as Jennifer Bailey, and she currently serves in a similar but lower-profile role of senior VP of government affairs. For another, the need for a full-time head of government affairs reflects the murky political waters Apple currently has to navigate.

Some pundits (including this one ) have speculated that this year’s biggest personnel change–Tim Cook stepping down as CEO–will see the current boss spend more time liaising with the White House, but even Cupertino’s most famous workaholic may not be able to handle the workload on his own.

Finally, Gurman reported last week that incoming CEO John Ternus will be rehiring Laura Legros, who served as a vice president of hardware engineering until she retired in 2022. Legros will assume a vice president role, “working cross-functionally with different parts of the company,” according to the report.

Legros was one of Ternus’ “most trusted deputies,” Gurman reports. In 2018, she appeared during an Apple event in New York to introduce an updated MacBook Air and was also front and center for the iPad Air design, two important products in Apple’s recent history.

One of the things tucked away in the small print of macOS 27 beta 3 is the news that you’ll need a 2TB iCloud+ subscription in order to use the new AI features for home security cameras in the Apple Home app.

While some are suggesting that we shouldn’t be too surprised by this, I do find it a somewhat disappointing move by Apple …

Apple announced significant AI-powered upgrades to the Home app at this year’s WWDC.

Intelligent Home app notifications

One of these was using Apple Intelligence to replace a whole sequence of individual security notifications with a single summary. At present, something as routine as a family member arriving home might generate a notification that they were seen in the driveway, then that the garage door was opened, then that the garage door was closed, then that they were seen at the front door, then that the front door was unlocked, and finally that it was locked.

In iOS 27, all of those individual notifications are replaced with a single one saying that the family member arrived home.

Three AI features for video footage

But the bigger improvements was an upgrade of HomeKit Secure Video from 1080p to 4K, and the use of Apple intelligence to analyze footage from home security cameras. Apple highlighted three intelligent capabilities.

With generated video descriptions, users can quickly understand what happened across a sequence of video clips, even without watching them. They can also search through camera clips so they can easily find what they’re looking for, like a package delivery. At the top of the Search page, the Home app elevates noteworthy clips that users may want to review, so they can quickly see important moments.

articles.title: Madden NFL 27 Review: A Franchise Mode With Some Football on the Side
articles.subtitle: Playing Madden all wrong feels so right After a torrid affair with the NCAA during my college years, I only really started following the NFL a few years ago when I was conscripted into my family’s fantasy football league.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Playing Madden all wrong feels so right

After a torrid affair with the NCAA during my college years, I only really started following the NFL a few years ago when I was conscripted into my family’s fantasy football league. Upon claiming back-to-back championships in 2022 and 2023, I felt like it was safe to say I was “pretty into football.” I willingly, sometimes even eagerly, watch entire games without having to be at a bar. If that’s not fandom, I don’t know what is.

As a professional video game enjoyer, perhaps I’ve coasted too long on the assumption that sports games were not for “people like me.” So with the launch of Madden NFL 27 just around the corner, I couldn’t help but wonder: Is there a place for a weeby Final Fantasy enthusiast among the stats-savoring armchair quarterbacks? Could I be a sports-game person?

After a couple hours, my answer to this question would have been “oh heavens no. ” The experience of playing Madden 27 often feels like information overload. At any given moment, you are utterly snowed in with too many options, too many statistics, too much data. In many ways, this is an unruly and hostile experience. Yet I keep coming back.

That’s mostly because Madden is effectively the only NFL game, and I am simultaneously resigned and determined to make it work — even if that means playing it in a way that largely runs counter to the developers’ intentions.

The experience immediately opens on a bum note. Booting up Madden 27 as a newbie feels like getting onboarded to Salesforce during your first week at a new job. You will be asked to agree to impossibly long terms of service in four-point font. You will be prompted, in an unnecessarily hostile way, to enter EA account login credentials that are not strictly necessary to proceed, but you are automatically assumed to have.

That deeply corporate onboarding experience gives way to a sin that no Final Fantasy game would ever dare attempt: assuming the majority of its audience has played most — if not all — previous installments of the series and therefore does not need even the barest refresher on the various modes or gameplay basics.

The logical part of your brain knows that all of this will become familiar and routine in a short time. The emotional part of your brain tells you it’s time to jump out the nearest window and run shrieking for the hills, Simpsons style.

I venture a peek into the settings menu, my first port of call when starting any new game. The UI is a never-ending Russian nesting doll of small white text. There are 12 submenus within the settings menu, so many that a single screen cannot contain them all. Within the penalties submenu alone are seven sliders for items like offensive holding and false start, on a scale of 0-99.

This is followed by an additional seven on-off toggles for stuff like “kick catch interference” and “running into the kicker. ” And this isn’t even the most granular of the 12 submenus: the Coach Adjustments menu alone features submenus within submenus, with dozens upon dozens of inscrutable options like “Cover 4: Quarters Check: 1 Rec Tight,” which itself has four possible selections.

All of this leaves me feeling as though I unintentionally stumbled upon evidence of a new boyfriend’s toggle and slider fetish. Oh brother, I don’t wanna see this! I realize all of these options are the product of painstaking developer work and a sincere love for the sport, but it’s all so cluttered and imposing, just begging for more approachable curation to help new and casual players find their footing.

Madden 27 ’s Ultimate Team Mode requires an online connection and hence would require me to make an EA account, to which I say a hearty “no thank you, I’m good” in light of recent events. So I set up a Franchise Mode save file, customizing my coach down to his Air Max 90s.

The immersive quarterback experience is the centerpiece of the Madden franchise, and there’s an evident reluctance to deviate too much from that. But Franchise Mode purports to offer more of what I’m looking for in a football video game — managing a roster of players, working within the salary cap, negotiating contracts, and calling plays in the heat of the moment. I’m far less interested in an intricate on-field sim than I am a front-office management sim, so this all sounds great to me.

It’s time to be brutally honest: I want a football game where I don’t actually have to play that much football. Could I make Madden NFL 27 feel more like Umamusume: Pretty Derby? Turns out, you kind of can.

Things started off strong as I sunk into setting up Franchise Mode. “Mr. Brightside” by The Killers began to play, a clean, fast pitch down the middle of the elder millennial strike zone. Things are improving! I want to enjoy this! I will learn valuable player insights that will prevent me from being suckered into drafting Christian McCaffrey for a third straight year in fantasy football because of his high ADP score!

I chose the Los Angeles Rams as my team, betraying my Bay Area roots because the Rams currently have Madden’s highest OVR score, I enjoy their QB Matthew Stafford, and frankly I wanted to make things easier on myself. As I tinker, I notice that the words “smoke,” “drag” and “dress” are omitted from Madden 27 ’s version of “Mr. Brightside.” If you’re familiar with the song, you’ll understand these are pretty load-bearing nouns. And just like that, I’m back to being annoyed.

Thankfully, it’s short-lived. As I begin the pre-season, several members of my squad want to renegotiate their contracts. New for Madden 27 is the Persona Engine, which gives every player a distinct personality profile, pulling from a pool of more than 65 traits. It aims to replace older scripted scenarios to make player reactions and contract negotiations feel more realistic.

My first time trying it out, I committed a colossal boner and lowballed star wideout Puka Nacua so egregiously that he stormed out of the negotiation, never to return. (I deserved it. ) I do wish the game gave you more context for whether you’re offering a player a good or bad deal, or at least made “negotiation insight” one of its 10,000 toggleable options.

articles.title: The Utility App Flood Won’t Last
articles.subtitle: The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.

Since then, veteran developers are releasing new apps and updating existing ones faster than ever, and new developers are releasing their first apps in droves. Today, supply is dramatically up, demand is flat, and quality is seemingly simultaneously up and down, depending on where you look.

How these forces play out long-term is anyone’s guess, but it’s worth examining because, just as Federico’s link to Bryan Irace’s post about agentic coding tools foreshadowed the rise of tools like Codex and Claude Code, today’s trends are sparks that have the potential to become tomorrow’s App Store wildfires or simply fizzle out.

Utility apps are on the front lines of this change. The TechCrunch story I linked in April picked up on this trend:

Another interesting tidbit from Appfigures is that the Utilities app category moved up the top five chart.

If anything, the trend has accelerated in the months since.

It’s not surprising at all that utility apps have taken off. They’ve been a staple of new developers since long before agents came along. That’s because many are UI wrappers around command line tools. That isn’t a knock against the developers of those apps; most users don’t want to open Terminal to convert a video or audio file to another format using ffmpeg, for example. By building a great UI around command line tools, developers have made them far easier to use.

However, the relative simplicity and narrow scope of many utility apps have made them a natural fit for AI agents, too. That’s why the App Store (and my inbox) is deluged with Mac menu bar and single-screen iPhone and iPad utility apps.

On the one hand, the abundance of utilities has been great for users. More choice means you’re more likely to find the app that perfectly fits your needs.

On the other hand, though, I don’t think what’s happening in the category is sustainable and expect to see it dramatically shift again in the coming months. As we’ve seen from reporting by The New York Times, app supply is outstripping demand by orders of magnitude, which will drive down prices. That alone is likely to cause the utility app market to shrink. But there’s more to it than that.

Remember, the demand shifts that The New York Times reported, based on Sensor Tower numbers, are for the entire App Store, where download numbers have grown 2-3% this year and last. I expect utility downloads to actually shrink in the coming months – again, because of agents.

Utilities, especially simple ones, are exactly the sorts of apps that are becoming trivially easy for power users – the very users these utilities are made for – to create themselves. From frontier labs‘ model improvements to a growing number of app-building tools from those same labs and third parties, it’s never been easier to build a web or native app yourself.

And although I agree with people, like Nilay Patel, who say the notion that everyone will build their own software is overblown, the utility market is different. Your average person is not downloading apps to adjust the frame rate and file format of a video or downloading YouTube videos to watch later.

But those are exactly the sort of things that people who are using agents are doing with them, whether they’re having an agent do those things directly via a command line tool in an app like Codex or Claude Code or building an app to do the same thing. That’s going to put even more pressure on the category.

That said, I think there will always be a cohort of users who would rather pay for an app than build it themselves, so I’m not predicting the demise of utilities in general – just the end of today’s frothy market. I also think there remains a place for simple utilities that solve hard problems with clever solutions. Not every utility is a UI wrapper for a terminal command. Plenty of apps feature original solutions or thoughtful and unconventional remixes of disparate tools.

Utilities aren’t going away, but just like other App Store deluges, the trend will recede. It’s just that this time, it’s likely to flip faster than usual.

articles.title: Siri will sometimes summarize webpages and videos from within Safari and YouTube apps
articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.title: Takoyaki At ‘Disastrous’ Deltarune Fan Event Leaves Attendees With Food Poisoning
articles.subtitle: What does Toby Fox’s episodic RPG Deltarune have in common with Fyre Festival, DashCon, and, most recently, the Glasgow Willy’s Chocolate Experience? If you haven’t been on Twitter the past few days, then you are (unfortunately) about to find out.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
What does Toby Fox’s episodic RPG Deltarune have in common with Fyre Festival, DashCon, and, most recently, the Glasgow Willy’s Chocolate Experience? If you haven’t been on Twitter the past few days, then you are (unfortunately) about to find out.

On Sunday, a Toronto event organizer called Sugar Packet hosted an unofficial Deltarune Fan Cafe event. According to the ticket website, attendees who paid $15 could spend 50 minutes in the cafe eating themed food, purchasing merchandise, posing in a photo booth, and entering a raffle. There was also a free portion of the event that offered a more fleshed-out artist alley and a live playthrough of the game’s newly released Chapter 5, which inspired the event’s theming and menu.

But all of this was almost entirely overshadowed by some glaring problems, the worst of which was a certain menu item. The cafe served takoyaki, presumably inspired by a vendor in Chapter 5’s festival who sells the same dish.

But according to the organizers, the event’s takoyaki was stored improperly and left in a cooler to thaw (and, as some attendees alleged, later left out of the cooler after ice ran out), which led to multiple cases of food poisoning that reportedly sent several attendees to urgent care or the hospital. It also just didn’t look too appetizing:

i was there…. the takoyaki tasted kinda undercooked 😭😭😭 pic.twitter.com/Xc3rZV0kRv — Loch 🖍️🦕 (@lochstep) August 12, 2026

i was there…. the takoyaki tasted kinda undercooked 😭😭😭 pic.twitter.com/Xc3rZV0kRv

— Loch 🖍️🦕 (@lochstep) August 12, 2026

In Deltarune’s Chapter 5, after taking a bite of the in-game takoyaki, party member Susie mentions that it tastes like “raw onion.” If nothing else, I guess the organizers of this event could be applauded for their commitment to the source material here?

Beyond that nasty-looking takoyaki, attendees also complained about overcrowding, issues with merch pre-orders, and unexpected pricing changes. Also, the whole thing was held in a sparsely-decorated college building:

this picture i took sums up the whole aura of the deltarune cafe 💗 chalk and pen on the ground, chalkboard for the students, and podium for the professor pic.twitter.com/tseLUjhHfi — sarah ⚢ (@lesbicot) August 12, 2026

Yes, even the alleged kitchen was just in a regular old classroom:

Several days after the event, the organizers apologized (via four separate Instagram posts), offered refunds, announced a plan to compensate attendees for any takoyaki-related hospital bills, and even offered information on how to report food safety violations to the city. They also announced a 10-month hiatus and encouraged attendees to refrain from harassing volunteers, with two named organizers taking full responsibility.

“The Deltarune cafe was a failure,” the organizers wrote on Instagram. It’s nice to see Sugar Packet taking accountability, at least? I just hope everyone makes a full recovery.

articles.title: Apple TV has lost the plot
articles.subtitle: Macworld The Apple TV 4K has long been cord-cutters’ go-to set-top box due to its ad-free experience, fluid performance, superior app quality, and much more.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
The Apple TV 4K has long been cord-cutters’ go-to set-top box due to its ad-free experience, fluid performance, superior app quality, and much more. Apple had been offering the 3rd-generation model for a tantalizing starting price of $129, with the maxed-out Ethernet variant going for $149. While there have always been cheaper options, at those prices, it was hard not to recommend Apple TV to anyone looking for a standalone set-top box.

However, following a significant price increase and stagnant innovation, this device has rapidly lost its appeal—making it challenging for newcomers to justify buying an Apple TV 4K. And from what the rumors say, it doesn’t look like the new model will make it much more compelling.

Make it make cents

Perhaps the Apple TV 4K 3’s biggest con is its updated, illogical pricing. The entry-level model now costs $199 while the pricier one sells (or doesn’t) for a whopping $249—a 67 percent increase and the most expensive it’s ever been. While it’s understandable to see iPad and Mac price hikes due to the memory crisis, the set-top box is four years old and packs a five-year-old A15 Bionic chip with just 4GB of RAM. It’s neither new nor powerful enough to justify such a crazy price bump.

For comparison, Google’s TV Streamer costs just $99, and there are a ton of more affordable TV sticks from Roku, Amazon, and others that get the job done for a fraction of the price. Unlike personal computing devices, smart TVs don’t heavily revolve around essential ecosystem integrations and personal data sync.

Most users exclusively rely on them to download streaming apps like YouTube, Netflix, Spotify, and Hulu. These services typically share the same main UI across different smart TV platforms and let you quickly sign in with any smartphone by simply scanning a QR code.

While nice to have, a pretty interface and the Apple ecosystem tie-in won’t be worth it for many budget-conscious iPhone users, especially when the app’s already on their other devices.

Siri-ous setbacks

In the age of AI, smart assistants are expected to be baked into all of our everyday devices. Despite costing 50 percent less than Apple TV 4K, Google’s TV Streamer has managed to port the Gemini experience, letting users control their big screens via speech, ask complex questions, and more. Amazon Fire TVs similarly offer an Alexa integration to assist viewers with various tasks.

When tvOS 27 arrives, Apple TV 4K will still ahve the old Siri.

Foundry

The latest Apple TV 4K, on the other hand, is still plagued by the outdated Siri, which can barely answer any meaningful questions or get anything done. It’s true that Apple Intelligence and the overhauled Siri AI require at least 8GB of RAM on iPhones, iPads, and Macs, but that didn’t not stop Apple from bringing Siri AI to 2023’s Apple Watch Series 9 with the S9 chip.

Granted, it needs an iPhone nearby, but it’s safe to assume nearly every Apple TV 4K will also have an iPhone connected to the same network.

Furthermore, the Apple TV 4K won’t need to generate Genmoji or index emails, messages, and documents, so it shouldn’t need as much memory as an iPhone. tvOS could’ve at least adopted the more conversational Siri with world knowledge and ChatGPT integration, as it heavily relies on cloud processing anyway and isn’t locally demanding. Its omission sends the wrong message to anyone who has or may be looking to buy an Apple TV 4K.

Playing games

The Siri exclusion would’ve been more tolerable had tvOS 27 introduced other noteworthy features that keep users engaged. Alas, tvOS was barely mentioned at WWDC, with its main highlights including AutoMix for Apple Music, a redesigned Podcasts app, and other minor enhancements. In fact, even Apple’s own OS 27 preview webpage fails to include a tvOS section. Adding the lack of AI and the dramatic price hike into the mix makes it hard to recommend the Apple TV 4K to customers.

You can play games on your Apple TV 4K, but it’s a far cry from a gaming machine.

articles.subtitle: MacPaw has announced a long-term strategic partnership with Liquid AI to co-develop an on-device AI technology stack built specifically for the Mac. The collaboration will start with Eney, MacPaw’s AI assistant for macOS.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
MacPaw has announced a long-term strategic partnership with Liquid AI to co-develop an on-device AI technology stack built specifically for the Mac.

The collaboration will start with Eney, MacPaw’s AI assistant for macOS.

MacPaw is teaming up with Liquid AI to bring more on-device AI to the Mac

Liquid AI’s Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) will be adapted for Mac-based assistance and combined with MacPaw’s own on-device technologies: Mnemos for memory and Elix for inference.

Eney already shifted to a local model last year, keeping reasoning, contextual search, skill execution, and conversation history on the device whenever possible.

The new partnership is intended to push that approach further. The two companies are jointly developing the underlying stack rather than MacPaw simply adding another third-party model.

Once the technology has been tested and implemented in Eney, MacPaw says it plans to bring it to more of its products. It also wants to make the shared AI stack available to Mac developers through Setapp.

That could let participating apps expose more of their capabilities and context to Eney. This would allow the assistant to understand what is inside an app. It could also provide more useful answers or take relevant actions.

You can learn more about MacPaw’s on-device AI technology and today’s announcement here, and catch up on Liquid AI here.

iPhone X

Apple today updated its vintage and obsolete product lists, with the iPhone X and 15-inch 2018 MacBook Pro now classified as obsolete. Here’s what that means.

iPhone X and 15” 2018 MacBook Pro now obsolete

In an update to its “ Obtaining service for your Apple product after an expired warranty ” support article, Apple today moved the 15-inch 2018 MacBook Pro and iPhone X from its vintage products lists to its obsolete products lists.

As Apple explains, once a device is added to its obsolete products list, the company discontinues all hardware service for it, and service providers can no longer order parts for it.

Products may become obsolete more than seven years after Apple stops distributing them for sale, though the actual timing of the classification is ultimately up to Apple.

Apple’s vintage list, on the other hand, includes products that the company will service only while parts remain available. Apple considers a product vintage when it stopped distributing it for sale more than five but less than seven years ago.

Apple dropped major OS support for the iPhone X with iOS 17, leaving iOS 16 as its final major release. The device currently tops out at iOS 16.7.16. The 15-inch 2018 MacBook Pro, meanwhile, is limited to macOS Sequoia, with macOS 15.7.7 currently available for the model.

Formerly indie developer Jason Weingardt, on Threads:

Some personal news: I’ve joined the team at Major League Baseball, and the Mosaic app has come with me. The last 3+ months have, without question, been the wildest of my life.

I’m beyond thankful to MLB for the chance to help shape how fans experience baseball, and even more thankful to the community of fans around the world who tried Mosaic, filed bug reports and feature requests, and helped shape it along the way. We believe Mosaic can be a valuable tool to help learn more about what fans want…. I will keep working on Mosaic as part of my job….

Most importantly: Mosaic is sticking around. Features may come and go, but my ask is that you continue to write in with your feedback about what you like, don’t like, and what you’d want to see in a baseball app. I’m excited for what’s next, and I hope you are too.

We believe Mosaic can be a valuable tool to help learn more about what fans want…. I will keep working on Mosaic as part of my job…. Most importantly: Mosaic is sticking around. Features may come and go, but my ask is that you continue to write in with your feedback about what you like, don’t like, and what you’d want to see in a baseball app. I’m excited for what’s next, and I hope you are too.

Mosaic is a baseball app that’s been in TestFlight for a few months. (Scroll back through Weingardt’s Threads history for details. ) From the moment I saw it, I was dazzled—it’s a great iOS baseball app that uses all of Apple’s platform technologies to lay out live game data and show off other MLB features in ways that MLB’s own app just doesn’t.

And it even integrated with MLB TV, so if you’re a subscriber to MLB’s premium video service, you can watch games via Mosaic, including in the most mind-blowing multiview I’ve seen.

I don’t want to lean too much into the current state of the official MLB app, but it used to be so cutting-edge and great that when I was at Macworld, we gave it a zillion awards and ended up just inducting it into our “app hall of fame.” But over the years, that app has become generic and unfocused and one-size-fits-all. It is no longer a joy to use.

So Jason Weingardt wrote Mosaic, by himself, and it’s a properly great iOS app (that also runs on iPad and Mac and, as of today, Apple TV). I ran into Weingardt at WWDC and he was so happy that people had already fallen in love with his own personal semi-secret passion project.

We all pretty much expected Mosaic to be crushed by MLB once it figured out what was going on. No matter that it was using public APIs and honoring MLB’s own premium content subscriptions, it just felt like the kind of thing that was too good to be true.

Instead, to their immense credit, MLB hired Weingardt, and Mosaic is now apparently a part of MLB’s digital strategy. I almost can’t believe it. It’s the best possible outcome for Weingardt, MLB, and baseball fans with Apple devices.

I’m so happy to think that MLB’s apps may now be on a trajectory to go back to where they belong—in the app hall of fame.

articles.title: Wispr Flow takes on AI meeting assistants with Notetaker, its first product beyond dictation
articles.subtitle: Wispr Flow users on Mac can now access Notetaker, an AI-powered meeting assistant that uses calendars, connected apps, and personal dictionaries to provide additional context for transcripts, summaries, and notes. Here are the details.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Wispr Flow users on Mac can now access Notetaker, an AI-powered meeting assistant that uses calendars, connected apps, and personal dictionaries to provide additional context for transcripts, summaries, and notes. Here are the details.

Wispr Notetaker now available for Mac

If you’re unfamiliar with Wispr Flow, it is one of the leading voice-to-text AI tools for a growing number of users who feel comfortable using voice to compose messages, emails, documents, and other text instead of typing.

Granted, voice-based interactions are not practical in every environment. Still, Wispr Flow ’s rapidly growing user base (which the company said in March was expanding by 40% month over month) suggests that AI-powered dictation tools may become mainstream faster than many expected, or give them credit for.

Until now, Wispr has offered a single product, which polishes up messy speech and turns it into “clear, polished writing in every app.”

Today, the company is expanding its lineup with Notetaker, a smart, AI-powered meeting assistant, transcriber, and summarizer. The new tool is built directly into Wispr Flow and appears as a new item in the app’s left-hand sidebar.

As Wispr CEO and co-founder Tanay Kothari notes (no pun intended):

“Nobody reads meeting transcripts. But everyone acts on them. The transcript feeds the summary, the summary feeds the follow-up email, the recap goes to whoever missed the call. You’ve learned to give the notes a quick once-over before trusting them, because sometimes a name is wrong or an action item is assigned to the wrong person.”

In other words, while the transcript itself may have limited value to some, accurately extracting the key details, decisions, and action items from it can be more useful to a broader set of users.

Notetaker also briefs users before meetings by gathering relevant information from their notes and the web, with each line linked to its source. More broadly, it draws context from calendars and connected apps such as Slack.

During meetings, Notetaker provides a live transcript so the user can quickly check back on what was said. Once the meeting ends, it processes the full recording again with additional context, which Wispr says improves the final transcript and the summaries, decisions, key dates, and action items generated from it.

Afterward, users can ask questions about their full meeting history, with answers linked to the moment when the relevant information was discussed. Notetaker can also catch users up on portions of a meeting they missed or were not paying attention to.

In addition to sharing Wispr Flow ’s custom dictionary, which helps with accuracy for acronyms, names, product names, and beyond, Wispr Notetaker “draws on the apps you connect, like Slack, and your calendar, to understand what this particular conversation is about,” says Kothari.

This also helps with automatic speaker attribution, which is particularly useful for meetings with several participants.

Wispr Notetaker transcribes meetings based on on-device audio capture, rather than joining calls as a separate participant.

It works across multiple meeting platforms, including Zoom, Google Meet, Teams, and Slack huddles, and has MCP support, allowing users to pull transcripts, summaries, and notes into Claude, ChatGPT, and custom agents or workflows.

Wispr Notetaker is available beginning today on Mac, with a Windows version in development.

articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation. Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. articles.title: After a public scrap between CEO and former writer, Saber Interactive finally adds AI disclaimer to Steam page and doubles down: 'AI can and should help shape gamer experiences'
articles.subtitle: It's been a wild ride.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
One of the unexpected stories this week has been that of a rather public spat between former Saber Interactive writer Stella Sacco, who claimed she was replaced in favour of AI, and the publisher's CEO, who tore into her via a statement sent to This Week in Videogames.

"Stella who?" asked Matt Karch, "I had to ask Claude because I have never spoken to her or seen her. We have already said we are using AI for certain parts of the game and will update the Steam page once we have finalized the feature set."

Karch also added that "it was always our intention to reveal this until Stella violated her confidentiality clause and revealed this before we were ready." Sacco, who claimed she was replaced "with ChatGPT" in 2023, called the statement "remarkably pathetic for the CEO of any company to be making."

You can read both parties' full statements in the articles linked above—the most recent development is that Saber Interactive has been seemingly pressed into adding a Steam AI disclaimer to the game's store page, which is present at the time of writing, but was notably not present when the game was put on the store on July 30.

"Once it's finalised we will update the Steam page," Karch told IGN. "In Rideshare we added an unrelated experimental mode to the game to play around with these concepts. "It's not the core experience. And even in this case it required us adding two writers and multiple coders to work with AI tools to try and get a reasonable result. Maybe we are bad at business but the net cost of incorporating these features was significantly higher than leaving them out."

Karch then goes on to say that "my PR team is always terrified by even broaching the subject but I would be happy to engage in a reasonable conversation about how AI can and should help shape gamer experiences."

The disclaimers in question make reference to not just these AI-generated dialogue, but also "a mix of radio stations featuring human-made music and AI-generated music. Stations containing AI-generated music are clearly labeled as such in the game."

Karch chalks up the entire debacle to a "publicity stunt… This person was removed from the project three years ago. We have actually increased our writing staff since 2023. If I wanted publicity for this little game though, then I guess I have Stella to thank for it."

The entire situation, to put it extremely lightly, is a bit of a mess—regardless of whether or not Saber's landed itself in troubled waters ( Sacco seems to think so ), if I were a videogame publisher, I might ask myself why I felt the need to wait to be "ready" to reveal something core about how my game was made, and why I might be making my PR team "terrified".

Could it be that AI is broadly unpopular with the gamers Saber Interactive is claiming to serve? Surely not.

articles.title: Apple Opens Houston Advanced Manufacturing Center Ahead of Mac Mini Production
articles.subtitle: Apple today opened its Advanced Manufacturing Center (AMC) in Houston, Texas. It's located in the same Houston facility where Apple makes AI servers and will start manufacturing the Mac mini this year.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Apple today opened its Advanced Manufacturing Center (AMC) in Houston, Texas. It's located in the same Houston facility where Apple makes AI servers and will start manufacturing the Mac mini this year.

Small and medium businesses can visit the 20,000-square-foot facility for free training and educational sessions, taking advantage of interactive labs, tools, and equipment, including a holographic lab table. Apple says participants can learn the "same innovative processes" used to make Apple devices.

"In less than nine months, we have invested hundreds of millions of dollars into this Houston facility. We stood up a factory, started production, and shipped the first advanced AI servers off the line. Today, we're thrilled to open our new Advanced Manufacturing Center, a place where businesses, workers, and students can learn the same innovative processes that we use to make Apple's most groundbreaking products.

And we're pleased to begin Mac mini production later this year," said Tim Cook, Apple's CEO. "We believe in American workers and American ingenuity, and we are moving at an incredible pace because we want to build more than great products. We want to build the future of American manufacturing. "

Apple experts will hold sessions on topics like advanced manufacturing principles for final assembly and design considerations for printed circuit board assembly, and lead interactive workshops that use the site's representative production facility and equipment. Apple says participants will learn to identify and adapt to production challenges in real time.

In the future, the AMC will offer hands-on training to local college students.

The location is part of Apple's pledge to spend $600 billion to support manufacturing in the United States. Businesses interested in visiting the AMC can sign up for notifications about future sessions on Apple's website.

articles.subtitle: A TerminalWidget shortcut action and its output. I’m a huge fan of displaying ambient information in my computer interfaces, which on my Mac tends to involve putting data about weather, solar power and the like in my menu bar, so it’s available at a...
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
I’m a huge fan of displaying ambient information in my computer interfaces, which on my Mac tends to involve putting data about weather, solar power and the like in my menu bar, so it’s available at a glance. My tool of choice for this is SwiftBar, itself a follow-on to BitBar (which has been rebooted as xbar ). On my iPad, I’ve been using custom widgets generated with Simon Støvring’s Scriptable app to do the job.

Now here’s a new contender that generates widgets on both Mac and iOS: Brett Terpstra’s $20 TerminalWidget, which lets you send data to a widget from a command-line script, Shortcut, AppleScript, or a URL scheme.

Widgets are more complicated than little items that live in the menu bar. That’s why Scriptable uses little JavaScript scripts to build them. TerminalWidget has a basic set of terminology that lets you target specific widgets and provides some pre-filled functionality that lets you generate some design elements without much hassle. It’ll also just… take text you give it and display it if you want.

If you’re working via Shortcuts, you can update TerminalWidget using a bunch of different template types: Chart, Image, Progress, Table, or Text. Just as with the command line, each Shortcuts action contains a bunch of variables, so you can customize colors and fonts, add a caption and title, or other things that help fill out TerminalWidget’s templates.

It’s by design a lot less flexible than something like Scriptable, where the sky’s the limit—but it’s also a lot more approachable, since you’re basically filling in the blanks with whatever data you want to provide.

I wasn’t really able to replicate my beloved Scriptable weather widget in TerminalWidget—not flexible enough—but TerminalWidget also supports straight-up image use, which allowed me to generate the contents of my Scriptable widget via script, output it as an image, and then tell TerminalWidget to load that image. So if you wanted to offload widget duties to your Mac or a remote server, you could do that and just display the image in TerminalWidget.

In a way, TerminalWidget turns its limitation (lack of flexibility) into a strength, because the learning curve is so gentle, especially if you use Shortcuts, which literally shows you every single possible variable you could possibly use, so you can tinker and figure out what you want to display. Dr. Drang is using it for planetary positions, because that tickles his fancy.

If there’s something you’d like to put on a glanceable widget across iPad, iPhone, and Mac, TerminalWidget will let you do it. That’s a beautiful thing. Now I need to figure out what widgets to add to my own devices…

It’s the end of a very short road for ChatGPT Atlas, OpenAI’s dedicated web browser for Mac. OpenAI has shared details about what happens when ChatGPT Atlas shuts down this weekend.

ChatGPT is the new ChatGPT Atlas

As we reported in July, OpenAI is discontinuing its standalone Atlas browser in favor of browser tools built into the new ChatGPT desktop app. Atlas is scheduled to stop working on August 9 following a brief wind-down period.

OpenAI warns that Atlas may no longer open, browse, or support agentic workflows after that date. Because the discontinued browser will not continue receiving security updates, users will want to move to a supported alternative.

The transition may require some manual housekeeping for some. Atlas bookmarks will not transfer automatically. OpenAI recommends exporting bookmarks as an HTML file and saving important pages before Sunday’s deadline.

Cookies may have export options where available. ChatGPT conversation history is stored separately and will remain available.

AI browser alternatives

OpenAI is directing users toward the new ChatGPT desktop app. Its built-in browser supports multiple tabs, downloads, website logins, autofill, password management, extensions, and persistent browser state. However, it’s not exactly a browser-first experience.

The company recommends its Chrome extension when a task requires an existing Chrome profile, signed-in session, open tabs, or other extensions. ChatGPT’s desktop app also includes a “computer use” functionality that can optionally let it control Safari when granted permission.

There are plenty of other AI browser options on the Mac, including Comet, Dia, Opera Neon, and Aside. Anthropic is taking a similar two-track approach: Claude Code offers a sandboxed in-app browser, while its Chrome extension can work with existing logged-in sessions.
